solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Pastry which French cook trimmed

parts.note: qui is the French word for which or who

indicators.note: trimmed means the word loses its tail end, here its final letter

parts.note: a chef is a cook

explanation.surface: A recipe question: which pastry did the French cook trim?
explanation.walkthrough: 'trimmed' cuts the last letter from CHEF, leaving CHE.
explanation.definitionFit: An egg-custard tart in a crust is a savoury pastry dish, so the general term covers it as an example.

clue.text: Daughter bypasses courtyard to teach some poetry

indicators.note: bypasses means goes round and skips, so the daughter letter is left out

parts.note: a quad is a quadrangle, a college courtyard
to train is to teach

explanation.surface: A daughter takes a detour round the college courtyard to teach some poetry.
explanation.definitionFit: A four-line stanza is a piece of verse, so it is some poetry.

clue.text: Writer's first article published is on family

parts.note: first is I, the Roman numeral one
an is the indefinite article
ran, as a newspaper ran a story, means published
kin means family

explanation.surface: A writer's first article has been published, featuring their family.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's of 'Writer's' stands for 'is', linking the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: He is a Scottish crime novelist, famous for the Rebus detective books.

clue.text: Have no stomach for fifth pork-pie?

parts.note: a pork-pie is a flat-crowned hat
E is the fifth letter, and the fifth vowel too

explanation.surface: Not having the stomach for a fifth pork pie.
explanation.walkthrough: The pork-pie is not food but a hat; a pork pie is a British cold pastry snack.
explanation.definitionFit: To detest something is to have no stomach or liking for it at all.

clue.text: Boozer circulates no.1 hotel in European resort

indicators.note: circulates suggests going round, so the pub word goes round the numeral

parts.note: a boozer is British slang for a pub, or bar
number one is I, the Roman numeral
the Ritz is a famous luxury hotel

explanation.surface: A pub drinker makes the rounds of a top hotel at a European holiday spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'circulates' puts I inside BAR, giving BIAR.
explanation.definitionFit: This town on the French Basque coast is a well-known seaside resort in Europe.

clue.text: Dicky rejected spacious European area of old

parts.note: dicky is British slang for unwell or ill

indicators.note: rejected means turned back, so the word reads upwards in this down light

parts.note: an airy room is spacious

explanation.surface: An unwell person turns down a spacious European area of times past.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dicky' is British slang for poorly, not a name; in a down light 'rejected' sends the airy word upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: This was an ancient region along the eastern Adriatic, the setting of Twelfth Night.

clue.text: She relates habit by motorists adopting improper tone

indicators.note: adopting means taking in, so the pair take the jumbled letters inside
by means beside, so the habit word sits next to the motorists

parts.note: the RAC, Royal Automobile Club, is a British motorists' organisation
use, as in custom, means habit

indicators.note: improper signals the word tone is rearranged

explanation.surface: A woman describes a habit motorists have of taking an improper tone.
explanation.walkthrough: The RAC is a British breakdown and motoring club. 'improper' scrambles the tone letters, which 'adopting' places between the club and the habit.
explanation.definitionFit: The feminine French form names a woman who tells stories well, a female narrator.

clue.text: The Italian accepts meadow's connected to part of canal

indicators.note: accepts means takes in, so the Italian article holds the meadow word

parts.note: il is the Italian word for the
a lea is a meadow; the 's means is

explanation.surface: The Italian accepts that a meadow is connected to part of a canal.
explanation.walkthrough: The canal is the alimentary canal, the gut, not a waterway.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes the ileum, the last stretch of the small intestine in the digestive tract.

clue.text: Stars here backed rally round in business zone

indicators.note: backed means the whole assembly is read in reverse, upwards in this down light
in signals the help word placed inside the business letters

parts.note: CO is the abbreviation for company, a business
to rally round is to aid or help

explanation.surface: Stars return to rally round in a business district.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rally round' is one phrasal verb meaning help, not a container signal; 'in' does that job, and 'backed' turns the whole assembly upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The belt of twelve astrological constellations is where these stars are found.

clue.text: Scot perhaps who paints disturbing masterpiece close to home

indicators.note: disturbing means breaking into, so the painter letters interrupt the gem word

parts.note: a gem is a masterpiece or treasure
RA is a Royal Academician, a painter

indicators.note: close to means the last letter of the word home

explanation.surface: A Scottish painter disturbs a masterpiece near home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'who paints' stands for a Royal Academician, whose initials crosswords use constantly; 'disturbing' means it breaks into the gem.
explanation.definitionFit: This spelling of the first name is typically Scottish, so it suggests a Scot by way of example.

clue.text: Plain tuna's sprinkled with bay leaf covering (not starter)

indicators.note: covering signals the trimmed bay word wrapped around the scrambled fish
not starter means the first letter is dropped

parts.note: the bay tree is the laurel, whose leaves make the victor's wreath

indicators.note: sprinkled suggests scattering, so the fish's letters are rearranged

parts.note: the word tuna, the 's being no letter, is the fodder

explanation.surface: Cooking instructions: plain tuna sprinkled with a bay leaf on top, minus the starter course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bay leaf' gives the tree's name, laurel, and 'not starter' beheads it; 'sprinkled' scrambles the fish, giving NATU, and 'covering' wraps the beheaded laurel around that.
explanation.definitionFit: The French phrase describes food cooked or served simply, without dressing, so it means plain.

clue.text: Articles available from language department

parts.note: Cree is a language of indigenous North American people

explanation.surface: Some articles are on offer from a university language department.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Articles' here means articles of faith, not newspaper pieces or grammatical words.
explanation.definitionFit: A statement of belief is set out as a list of articles of faith.

clue.text: Trio gains, regularly picking out horse?

indicators.note: regularly picking out means taking every second letter from the words

explanation.surface: A trio of punters wins regularly by picking out the right horse.
explanation.walkthrough: The even letters of TRIO GAINS are R, O, A, N.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a horse with a coat of mixed white and coloured hairs; the question mark admits it is a colouring as much as an animal.

clue.text: Fuel sustains Tyneside lads, half dancing this?

indicators.note: sustains means holds up, so the fuel word holds the region letters inside

parts.note: petrol is motor fuel
NE stands for the North East of England, where Tyneside is

indicators.note: half signals the first half of the word lads

explanation.surface: Fuel keeps Newcastle lads going while they dance, half-cut.
explanation.walkthrough: Tyneside is the Newcastle area of north-east England, hence the region's two-letter abbreviation; 'sustains' means the fuel holds it.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a Scottish country dance, so it is what you might be dancing.

clue.text: One watches pair getting fruity pie full of this?

definitions.meaning: an unwanted third person tagging along with a courting couple
a sharp green berry that fills a fruit pie

explanation.surface: A spectator watches a pair eating a fruit pie full of this.
explanation.walkthrough: To play this means to be the third wheel on a couple's date.
explanation.definitionFit: The berry is a fruit for pies, and British idiom uses it for the unwanted third party with a couple.

clue.text: It's annoying when church defaced roughly?

indicators.note: defaced means losing the face, here the front letter of the word

parts.note: kirk is the Scottish word for a church
some, as in some twenty people, means roughly or about

explanation.surface: Someone complains that it is annoying when a church is roughly vandalised.
explanation.walkthrough: 'defaced' takes the first letter off KIRK, leaving IRK.
explanation.definitionFit: Something tiresome and irritating is annoying; both are adjectives for what bothers you.

clue.text: Glimpse child's head during game with mirror

parts.note: to ape someone is to mirror or copy them

indicators.note: during signals the letter sits inside the game abbreviation

parts.note: RU is rugby union, a game

indicators.note: head means the first letter of the word child's

explanation.surface: A child gets a glimpse of their head while playing a game with a mirror.
explanation.walkthrough: 'during' puts C, the head of 'child's', inside RU.
explanation.definitionFit: The French loan word means a quick insight or brief view, much like a glimpse.

clue.text: Cleaner loads the empty dessert dish

parts.note: a char is a British cleaning lady, a charwoman
a lot means loads

indicators.note: empty means the word the loses its middle letter

explanation.surface: A cleaner loads the empty dessert dish into the dishwasher.
explanation.walkthrough: 'empty' leaves TE from 'the'.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a pudding of fruit baked or set inside a lining of bread or sponge fingers.

clue.text: Social occasion seen in Assam and Charleston?

parts.note: Assam is a variety of tea
the Charleston is a 1920s dance; the question mark flags an example

explanation.surface: A social event is found in the Indian state of Assam and the US city of Charleston.
explanation.walkthrough: Assam and Charleston look like places but are a tea and a dance.
explanation.definitionFit: An afternoon gathering with tea and dancing is a social occasion.

clue.text: Concerned, Alan gets turkey gutted thoroughly

indicators.note: gutted thoroughly means every one of the three words loses its insides, keeping only its ends

explanation.surface: A worried Alan gets a turkey and guts it thoroughly.
explanation.walkthrough: Each word keeps only its outside letters: AN, GS and TY.
explanation.definitionFit: Being full of anxiety and worry is close to being concerned; the slang word describes troubled feelings.

clue.text: Second person raising electronic objection somewhere on the web

parts.note: you is the second-person pronoun

indicators.note: raising means lifting up, so the pair read upwards in this down light

parts.note: but is an objection, as in no ifs or buts

explanation.surface: A second person raises an electronic objection online.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raising' turns E plus BUT upwards, making TUBE.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a video-sharing website, a specific place you can visit on the internet.

clue.text: Pink eggs collected back in woods to consume

indicators.note: collected means gathered in, so the fish-egg word takes the letter inside

parts.note: roe is fish eggs

indicators.note: back in points to the final letter of the word woods

parts.note: to eat is to consume

explanation.surface: Pink eggs gathered in the woods, ready to be eaten.
explanation.walkthrough: 'collected' takes in two pieces at once: the back of 'woods' and the verb for consume, split the fish-egg word apart.
explanation.definitionFit: The word describes a rosy colour, a shade of pink.

clue.text: Tiny bird initially ignored private celebrity

indicators.note: initially ignored means the first letter is left off

parts.note: a wren is a tiny bird
own, as in one's own room, means private

explanation.surface: A tiny bird was ignored at first by a private celebrity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initially ignored' drops W from WREN, leaving REN.
explanation.definitionFit: Fame and wide acclaim are what celebrity means as an abstract noun.

clue.text: He gets a buzz touring French island northwards

indicators.note: touring means going round, so the buzz word surrounds the island

parts.note: a hum is a buzz

indicators.note: northwards means going up, so the word reads upwards in this down light

parts.note: ile is French for island

explanation.surface: A man gets a thrill touring a French island heading north.
explanation.walkthrough: 'He' looks like a man but is the chemical symbol. 'northwards' reverses ILE to ELI; 'touring' puts HUM around it.
explanation.definitionFit: He is the chemical symbol for this light noble gas, element two.

clue.text: Coastal town boats, foolishly open to all, besieged by seabird

indicators.note: besieged by means surrounded by the bird word

parts.note: the erne is a sea eagle

indicators.note: foolishly signals the word boats is rearranged

parts.note: U is the British film rating for universal, suitable for all

explanation.surface: Boats foolishly left open to everyone are besieged by a seabird on the coast.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a seaside town in Sussex, on England's south coast; 'open to all' is the British U film certificate. 'foolishly' gives ASTBO, and 'besieged by' wraps the bird around it.
explanation.definitionFit: This Sussex seaside resort sits on the English Channel coast.

clue.text: Less risky when putting back iron right?

indicators.note: putting back means turning round, so the word is read in reverse

parts.note: as means when, as in as I left
Fe is the chemical symbol for iron

explanation.surface: Is it less risky to put the iron back on the right?
explanation.definitionFit: The comparative of secure means with less danger, so less risky.

clue.text: Jerk line amid fish

indicators.note: amid means in the middle of the fish word

parts.note: cod is a fish

explanation.surface: An angler jerks the line among the fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jerk' is a noun for a stupid person, not a tug on the line.
explanation.definitionFit: A dull, foolish person can be called a jerk or a lump-headed oaf; both are insults.

clue.text: Steps lead to jet setter's

indicators.note: lead to means the leading, first letter of the word jet

parts.note: the setter has, from the setter's view, is I've

explanation.surface: Steps lead up to the jet-setter's plane.
explanation.walkthrough: 'setter's' expands to setter has, written I've.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a lively swing dance, so as a noun it is a set of dance steps.

clue.text: Current judge retired to make conclusion

parts.note: in means fashionable or current

indicators.note: retired means drawn back, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: a ref, short for referee, judges a match

explanation.surface: The sitting judge has retired to reach a conclusion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current' is the fashionable sense, not electricity.
explanation.definitionFit: To deduce something from evidence is to reach or make a conclusion.

clue.text: Traditional nutrient somehow arrests onset of wind

indicators.note: arrests means holds or seizes, so the rearranged letters hold the W inside
somehow signals the word nutrient is rearranged
onset of means the first letter of the word wind

explanation.surface: A nutrient somehow stops wind from starting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'somehow' rearranges NUTRIENT; 'arrests' puts W, the onset of 'wind', inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Customs passed on by habit rather than written law are traditional, like an unwritten rule.

clue.text: Swimmer from Glasgow always put in extra length

indicators.note: put in means the Scots word is placed inside the word for extra

parts.note: more means extra
aye is a Scots word for always

explanation.surface: A Glasgow swimmer always puts in an extra length.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from Glasgow' marks a Scots word: there 'aye' can mean always as well as yes.
explanation.definitionFit: This long snake-like fish of tropical reefs swims, so it fits the playful term swimmer.

clue.text: Linguistics unit, ie lecturer and author, hold English course

indicators.note: hold means the two letters around the river name keep it inside

parts.note: the setter or author refers to themself as me
the Exe is a river in Devon, the course of a river being its path

explanation.surface: A lecturer and author run an English course in linguistics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'English course' looks academic but is a river course: the River Exe in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Linguists use the term for a basic meaningful unit of vocabulary, such as run covering runs and ran.
